name: Vejoz
confidence_why: Nercesian's reference grammar (2011, 2014) and Terraza and Cayré Baito (2014), working from separate Wichí communities, both place a single word-level stress on the final syllable, and Hunt (1913) reported the same final-syllable tendency for Vejoz itself, so Tovar's (1981) claim that accent belongs to the phrase rather than the word stands alone as an impressionistic note appended to a text collection.

new_statements.quote: El wichí organiza las sílabas de la palabra fonológica en pies yámbicos binarios de izquierda a derecha. La lengua es insensible al peso por tanto sílabas CV y CVC son consideradas indistintamente como sílabas livianas para la asignación del acento. Éste sigue un patrón rítmico, se aplica al núcleo del pie más a la derecha de la palabra fonológica. [...] No existen palabras básicas con más de tres sílabas. (p. 171) [...] Nótese que, dado que la división en pies es iterativa, las palabras con un número impar de sílabas tienen un pie monosilábico al final de la palabra fonológica. El acento secundario parece caer en sílabas alternantes de izquierda a derecha. (p. 172)
new_statements.translation: Wichí organizes the syllables of the phonological word into binary iambic feet from left to right. The language is weight-insensitive, so CV and CVC syllables are treated alike as light syllables for stress assignment. Stress follows a rhythmic pattern: it is applied to the head of the rightmost foot of the phonological word. [...] There are no basic words of more than three syllables. [...] Note that, since foot division is iterative, words with an odd number of syllables have a monosyllabic foot at the end of the phonological word. Secondary stress appears to fall on alternating syllables from left to right.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Vejoz has an empty rule; the thesis supplies one: weight-insensitive LR iambic feet with primary stress on the rightmost foot head (= final syllable of the phonological word), plus alternating secondary stress, extrametrical Class I suffixes and root-initial stress in noun incorporation. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted because the catalog states no placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iterative binary iambic feet built left to right over the phonological word, quantity-insensitive (CV = CVC, both light); primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot, which in every cited basic and affixed/cliticized/compounded word is the final syllable (ten.té 'stone', ?i.nót 'water', mi.tsí 'cat', ?a.tsi.ná 'woman', po.tsé.láj 'Pleiades', ?is.ti.wín 'eagle'; affixation moves primary stress to the new rightmost foot). The head vowel of each foot is lengthened (non-contrastively).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternating syllables from left to right (the heads of the non-final iambs); with an odd number of syllables the last foot is monosyllabic and a stress clash is perceived at the end of the word (p. 172, exx. 70-71).
new_statements.exceptions: Two morphologically conditioned exceptions (§4.2.2): (a) Class I locative/directional/instrumental suffixes (-ej 'INS', -hu 'inside', -a 'near', -e 'far', -ey 'very far', -kwe/-che directionals) are extrametrical: 'no son contabilizados en la division métrica y por tanto, nunca reciben acento a pesar de encontrarse en el último pie a la derecha de la palabra fonológica' (p. 187), so a word ending in one of them is stressed on the syllable before the suffix; Class II locatives/directionals (-pe', -fwi, -hi, -pho, -cho) are counted and can bear stress. (b) Noun incorporation (V+N) builds two unbounded feet bounded by the internal morpheme boundary, with stress by the root-stress rule (Hayes 1995: 32) on the first syllable of each root, e.g. i.wú.ló.me.ta 'he/she preaches' (p. 183). Vowel lengthening of foot heads is metrical, not contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Nercesian 2011 describes the Bermejo (bermejeño) variety of Wichí, specifically the 'abajeños del Bermejo' group of Formosa (Las Lomitas, Laguna Yema, Pozo del Mortero, J. G. Bazán, Pozo del Tigre, barrios of Ing. G. N. Juárez) and Chaco (Sauzalito, Nueva Pompeya, Pozo del Sapo), stated on thesis p. 20 and in §2.5 ('variedad estudiada en esta tesis', p. 61 region of vol. 1). This is the Bermejo/Vejoz lineage that Glottolog files under wich1263 (Hunt 1913 'El Vejoz o Aiyo' is the same river-Bermejo variety), not the Pilcomayo (Wenhayek/Weenhayek) or Salta upriver varieties; Nercesian notes (p. 49) that Terraza 2009 describes the Rivadavia (Salta) variety separately.

sources.quote: 'The stress pattern of Wichí is quantity-insensitive; that is, primary stress falls on the rightmost syllable of the word regardless of syllable weight (Cayré Baito 2013)' ... 'the stress pattern is not modified by the suffixes or enclitics that are added to the stem. Moreover, none of the prefixes affect the stress pattern and they are themselves always unstressed' ... 3.2.1 'there is one primary stress per word assigned to the rightmost syllable'. Fn. 9: 'stress in Wichí requires a thorough study, since it does not always appear to be regular ... some suffixes present a double behavior'. Ter
sources.note: Only modern statement for a Salta/Bermejo-arribeño variety (Rivadavia Banda Sur) near Tovar's Vejoz: word-level, quantity-insensitive, final primary stress; weakens the Tovar phrase-only leg of the CONFLICT.
